analysis.one_liner: Taxes investment gains of households with over $100 million in income or $1 billion in assets annually, like wages.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2025 with 33 Democratic cosponsors, the Billionaires Income Tax Act has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or vote ever since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require people earning more than $100 million a year, or holding more than $1 billion in assets, to pay income tax on their investment gains every year, even if they never sell. It targets strategies like "buy, borrow, die," where a wealthy person lives off loans against unsold stock and never pays income tax, then passes the assets to heirs who sell them tax-free. It also closes roughly 30 other loopholes available only to these taxpayers. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and has had no action since.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary wage earners, whose pay is taxed every payday under withholding, gain a tax code that treats the largest fortunes the same way. The bill's stated purpose is to require billionaires to pay tax annually "just like working people do on their income from wages" and to shut down borrowing against unsold assets as a tax-free way to fund lifestyles. A broader tax base could also reduce pressure to raise taxes on everyone else, though the bill does not earmark its revenue for any specific use.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires "applicable taxpayers" — individuals with income above $100 million (or assets above $1 billion, measured after debt) for three straight years — to recognize gains on tradable assets like stock each year as if sold at fair market value, instead of deferring tax indefinitely until sale.

For hard-to-price, nontradable assets like stakes in private companies, the bill instead charges a "deferral recapture amount" — interest on the tax that would have been owed each year — when the asset is finally transferred, so years of deferral are no longer free.

The bill ends the step-up in basis at death for applicable taxpayers: assets passed at death, by gift, or in trust are treated as sold at fair market value, closing the "buy, borrow, die" path where heirs sell inherited assets completely tax-free. Spousal transfers and charitable gifts are exempted.

The bill closes other loopholes for these taxpayers, including limits on like-kind exchanges, elimination of deferral on certain deferred compensation and private-placement life insurance, treatment of expatriates who renounce citizenship to escape U.S. tax for 10 years, and restrictions on qualified opportunity fund investments.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals earning over $100 million a year or holding over $1 billion in assets, plus trusts with over $10 million in income or $100 million in assets. Private companies, partnerships, and other pass-through businesses they own at least 5% of (or with over $50 million in their nontradable stakes) face new annual reporting duties. Tax and wealth-management advisers would pick up substantial new compliance work.

drawbacks.text: Mark-to-market tax applies to gains on assets the taxpayer has not sold, so a taxpayer can owe a large tax bill in a year when no cash came in; the bill softens this only partially, allowing first-year liability on nontradable assets to be paid in five annual installments and charging interest rather than immediate tax on hard-to-sell assets.

Valuing nontradable assets is hard. The bill relies on a hierarchy of values — original cost, adjusted basis, financial-statement values, values used to secure loans — plus Treasury anti-avoidance regulations, which invites years of valuation disputes between taxpayers and the IRS.
Pass-through entities owned by applicable taxpayers face new notice, reporting, and gain-allocation obligations, adding compliance costs and complexity for the businesses themselves.

Because the rules cover expatriates for 10 years after renouncing citizenship and direct the Treasury to write anti-avoidance rules, the bill anticipates — but may not fully prevent — wealthy taxpayers relocating or restructuring assets abroad before and after it takes effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is straightforward and narrow in scope: roughly the richest few thousand households would pay tax on investment gains the way workers pay on wages, and their heirs could no longer sell inherited assets tax-free. The main costs are complexity — valuing private companies annually, managing tax bills on unsold assets, and heavier reporting for businesses these households own — which fall almost entirely on the affected taxpayers and their advisers, not on ordinary filers. The genuine risks are administrative (valuation disputes, avoidance planning) rather than a broad cost to the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on September 17, 2025 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the Billionaires Income Tax Act on September 17, 2025, joined by 28 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The bill has 33 cosponsors, all Democrats; no Republican has signed on.
Since the September 17 referral, the action history shows no hearings, markups, or floor action.

Because the 119th Congress runs through January 2027, the bill technically remains alive, but with the House majority held by the party with zero cosponsors and no committee movement, it has no realistic path to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers with more than $100 million in annual income or more than $1 billion in assets are better off as things stand: the current rules that let them defer tax indefinitely on unsold investments and pass assets to heirs tax-free remain in place, at no cost to them, because the bill has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Billion-dollar households, who keep the status quo

against.what_they_did: No Republican members cosponsored the bill, and the majority has not brought it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on; with Republicans holding the House majority and the Ways and Means chairmanship, the bill has not moved past referral.

industries.industry: Households with over $1 billion in assets or $100 million in annual income
industries.note: The bill's entire point is to end their ability to defer income tax indefinitely through buy-borrow-die planning and tax-free inherited gains. Their continued benefit under the status quo comes at the cost of a tax code that taxes wages annually but lets the largest unrealized fortunes go untaxed for generations.

industries.industry: Closely held businesses and pass-through entities owned by applicable taxpayers
industries.note: Partnerships, S corporations, and other pass-throughs at least 5% owned by covered taxpayers (or holding over $50 million of their nontradable interests) must file notices, report gains and holding periods annually, and make basis adjustments. Small businesses not owned by covered taxpayers are untouched.

industries.industry: Tax advisory, valuation, and wealth management services
industries.note: Annual mark-to-market valuation of private assets, entity reporting, and expatriate rules would generate substantial new compliance and valuation work. Much of the same industry currently earns fees structuring the deferral strategies the bill would close.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican support, no committee hearing, and more than a year left in the Congress, the bill will most likely remain in Ways and Means and expire without a vote at the end of the 119th Congress, as most majority-opposed tax bills do. Its ideas could resurface in a future Congress or in a Democratic tax platform.
